generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, the common presentation errors show up in any subject's talks. Reading dense slides word for word loses the audience; overrunning means the part that matters most gets rushed; a slide crammed with detail splits attention from the speaker. Each error is fixable before the day, and the fix is usually less work, not more: fewer words on a slide, one clear figure, a rehearsal to time. Spotting the error is most of the cure.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students giving the same presentation to the same group.

Student A has strong material but faces the screen and reads each slide aloud. The slides are full of detail, the talk runs several minutes over, and the part that matters most is rushed to make up time. The group follows the slides, not the speaker, and the main point is lost in the overrun. The content deserved better than its delivery.

Student B gives the same content but has checked it against the common errors. The slides are cut to prompts and one clear figure, so the talk is to the audience, not the screen. It has been rehearsed to time, with a point planned to drop if needed, so the conclusion lands cleanly. The group follows the argument, and the message stays with them.

The material was identical. Only Student B corrected the errors that would otherwise have undone it.
generatedProse.summary: Good content can still be undone by a few common errors: reading the slides, overrunning, overloaded slides, and losing the audience. Each one is fixable before the day, and spotting it is most of the cure. You can now identify these errors, tell them apart from sound delivery choices, and correct them. With a fitting approach, a supporting structure and the errors in check, you are ready to deliver well.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Student B do that corrected the errors?

items.text: Cut the slides to prompts and one clear figure, and rehearsed to time with a point to drop.
Added more detail to the slides so nothing was forgotten.
Spoke faster to fit all the material in.
Faced the screen so the slides could be read in full.

feedback.correct: That's right. Cutting the slides to prompts and a clear figure, and rehearsing to time, corrected the errors.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the corrections that fixed the reading and the overrun.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B cut the slides to prompts and one figure and rehearsed to time, with a point to drop. More detail, speaking faster or facing the screen are the errors, not fixes.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
